threat_assessment:
At bracket 4 your cover story is the deck's own reputation. Five-colour Dragons reads as battlecruiser: the table budgets its answers for a turn-8 Ur-Dragon and a pile of 6-drops, and your first four turns — ramp, fixing, a modal 3-drop — confirm the story. The goldfish says the story is even true of the commander: mean cast 8.967, 0.0% by turn 6. Nobody watching for The Ur-Dragon is watching the actual clock.

The actual clock is Aggravated Assault. All three of your contained two-card infinites route through that single enchantment (deck-facts: Assault plus Savage Ventmaw, Old Gnawbone, or Cavern-Hoard Dragon), and two of the three are checker-verified. Ventmaw self-funds at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003). Gnawbone banks net +2 Treasures per unblocked cycle and kills the table sequentially — opponents dead on combats 6 and 12 (stack 006). The Cavern-Hoard line is still a candidate that needs a stack scenario; do not present it as fact.

That concentration is also your single point of failure: one Naturalize effect turns off every infinite at once, and the deck has no second extra-combat effect. So sequence Assault like a combo piece, not a value enchantment (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window). It comes down the turn it wins — Treasures or lands already able to pay {3}{R}{R}, a Ventmaw or Gnawbone connecting that combat — or it stays in hand.

Remember the funding trap deck-facts flags. Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, and an attacking Klauth — five sources — all make spells-only mana, and none of it can ever pay Assault's activation, because an activated ability is not a spell. Treasures are the legal wallet (stack 006), and Atsushi, the Blazing Sky is your walking bank: his death makes three unrestricted Treasures that pay the {3}{R}{R} without apology.

What bracket-4 tables answer first, in order: Aggravated Assault on sight; Miirym, because everyone has felt the Panharmonicon doubling (stack 002); Sneak Attack, because {R} for Drakuseth is a rate nobody forgives (stack 005); then Dragon Tempest once your board is wide (stack 001).

Your protection budget exists for exactly one turn — 66.0% of games it is in hand by turn 6. Deflecting Swat is the flagship: free while you control a commander, and the only card that answers the removal spell aimed at Assault mid-combo. Hold it for that job. Do not spend it saving a Signet's worth of value.

Embrace archenemy status in precisely two spots. One: the turn Assault is live with a connecting dragon. Two: any turn a damage-based sweeper is likely with Wrathful Red Dragon out — stack 004 verified Blasphemous Act into three of your Dragons redirecting 39 at one opponent's face. Be honest with yourself about that second one: it kills a player, not a table, and two triggers is only 26. It is deterrence and a one-player execution, not a win button.

Every other turn, stay small. Deploy in waves, let the Selesnya-shaped boards draw the wrath, and let the table keep aiming at a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.
matchups:
VS SWEEPER CONTROL: Wrath-math discipline (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math) — with a verified inversion clause in your pocket. Your mean board is thin anyway, 1.5 bodies by turn 6 (goldfish 1.463), so wave deployment costs you little. With Wrathful Red Dragon out, every DAMAGE sweeper is a trap for them: Blasphemous Act into three Dragons is 39 redirected at one face (stack 004, verified). Know the boundary — Wrathful triggers on damage dealt to your Dragons, and destroy-all or exile-all wraths feed it nothing.

Your rebuild is structurally cheap, and that is your edge. Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Temur Ascendancy, and Garruk's Uprising are enchantments the wrath never touches. Atsushi, the Blazing Sky dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures — mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault. Eminence discounts every recast, and Hellkite Courser rents the commander out of the untouchable zone for one hasty, draw-two attack (stack 005's refutation names Courser as the deck's real commander cheat). Hold one of Teferi's Protection / Heroic Intervention / Flawless Maneuver — in hand 66.0% of games by turn 6 — for the board that actually wins, not the board that merely looks nice.

VS STAX/TAX: You are forced into the beatdown seat, and you are built for it. Taxes punish your 5-7 shelf (23 cards), but three things break the math. Eminence discounts accrue from the command zone, where permanent-hate cannot reach. Treasure bursts (Goldspan, Old Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard) pay taxes in lump sums. And the Assault engines need exactly one clean combat — Ventmaw's loop is self-funding at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), so a single resolved activation goes over any incremental lock. Aim your sparse removal (Generous Gift, Chaos Warp, Swords) at the piece that stops combats or untaps — a Winter-Orb effect hurts far less than anything taxing activated abilities, because Assault is the whole exit.

VS AGGRO: You are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown), and the math loves you: roughly 120 combined life stands behind three defenses, and your fliers blank ground boards. Develop on schedule — ramp or fixing is in hand by turn 6 in 71.6% of games. Treat Crux of Fate as the sweeper that spares every Dragon you own, and Blasphemous Act with Wrathful out as a kill on the aggro player, not just a reset (stack 004). Do not race; your engine owns the long game.

VS COMBO: Answer-economy (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Your suite is Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, Deflecting Swat (free with a commander), Chaos Warp, and Teferi's Protection as the fold-proof out. Spend them at the win attempt, never earlier. You also race credibly: your own two-card lines assemble at low mana, so the mirror-frame is dueling pivot windows, not pure reaction. The pilot's white-less, token-heavy pods (pilot_feedback.md) mean opposing interaction skews toward counters and creature removal, not Silence-effects — plan around stack fights, not taxes on the combo turn.

GRAVEYARD HATE (against you): shrug. Patriarch's Bidding, Rivaz, and Haven recursion are bonuses, not the spine — a Bojuka Bog costs you a spell's worth of value, nothing structural. Your own Bidding is at its best in exactly the pilot's token pods: tokens never hit graveyards as cards, so the symmetry clause returns you a fistful of Dragons and them almost nothing.
how_it_wins:
The table looks at a nine-mana commander in five colours and files you under slow. Let them. Your engine has been running since your first upkeep — eminence takes {1} off every other Dragon spell from the command zone, and nothing has to resolve for that to be true.

So stop building turns around the commander. The simulator puts his mean cast at turn 8.967 and his cast-by-turn-six rate at 0.0%; cast the discounted Dragon instead, every single time. He is a luxury you take when nine mana is spare, never a plan you wait on.

Stack the reducers and the curve stops being a curve. Dragonspeaker Shaman takes {2} off, Urza's Incubator another {2}, Herald's Horn {1} and a look at the top of your library. Two of those down and Terror of the Peaks is a three-mana play, while Korlessa, Scale Singer casts Dragons off the top so your hand is not your only hand.

The fair kill is critical mass, and the order is the whole trick: payoff first, Dragon second. Dragon Tempest, Scourge of Valkas and Terror of the Peaks pay per Dragon entering and pay nothing for the ones already down. Land Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm before your top end and every nontoken Dragon after her comes with a copy — one Lathliss under her and Panharmonicon is 64 damage across twelve targets (stack 002).

The unfair kill is Aggravated Assault, and three contained two-card infinites run through that one enchantment — which is exactly why the computed floor reads bracket 4. Old Gnawbone funds the activation out of Treasures at net +2 a cycle and kills the whole table (stack 006); Savage Ventmaw's attack mana pays it with {R} left over (stack 003). So protect the enchantment, not the commander, and never cast it early to look busy. It is your loudest tell, and a bracket-4 table kills it on sight.

One trap will cost you a game if you let it. Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw and an attacking Klauth all make spells-only mana, and an activated ability is not a spell — none of it pays Assault's {3}{R}{R}. Count real mana before you swing, and lean on Treasures: Goldspan Dragon, Old Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard Dragon and a dying Atsushi, the Blazing Sky all pay for anything.

Early, you are the value seat, and you should enjoy it. Ramp, fix, hold Deflecting Swat and a protection spell, and let someone louder eat the removal. Then take one window: Hellkite Courser rents your commander out for a hasty attack, Sneak Attack drops Drakuseth for {R} (stack 005), Wrathful Red Dragon turns the next sweeper into a 39-point execution (stack 004). Take the turn that wins, not the turn that impresses.

combo_lines.001: The clause that decides this is one word in Miirym's trigger: nontoken. Fifteen Faerie Dragons arrive on a single instruction, and not one of them qualifies — she copies nothing. Dragon Tempest carries no such reservation, and CR 603.2c turns one event with fifteen occurrences into fifteen separate triggers, each reading the board fresh at its own resolution (CR 608.2h). The holding: seventeen damage, fifteen times, targets locked in independently, with priority passing between every instalment.
combo_lines.002: Panharmonicon does not care what a trigger says. Its clause asks only what caused the trigger — an artifact or creature entering — so Miirym's 'nontoken Dragon' and Terror of the Peaks's 'another creature' are treated alike, and each triggers an additional time (CR 603.2d). What keeps the cascade finite is the word that bounded the last one: the copies are tokens, and every nontoken clause in the chain steps over them. The holding: one six-mana cast, two nonlegendary Lathliss copies, and 64 damage in twelve separately aimed instances.
combo_lines.003: Ventmaw's second sentence is an express override of the emptying rule. 'Until end of turn, you don't lose this mana as steps and phases end' displaces CR 106.4, so the attack mana walks out of combat and into your postcombat main phase intact. CR 107.4b finishes the argument: generic costs accept any type, so {G}{G}{G} pays Assault's {3}. The holding: one attack funds one extra combat and leaves a mana behind. Nothing in the rules bounds the loop — blockers, removal and the sorcery-speed restriction do.
combo_lines.004: The doctrine on the record is CR 113.7a: once triggered, an ability exists independently of its source, and destroying that source afterwards does not touch it. Three Dragons you control are dealt 13 in one event, so Wrathful triggers three times — and the lethal-damage check (CR 704.5g) empties the battlefield before any target is chosen, leaving players as the only legal ones. Each dead Dragon still deals its 13, by last known information. The holding: 39 damage, all of it assignable to a single opponent, and never enough for two.
combo_lines.005: Two zones settle this. Sneak Attack reaches 'a creature card from your hand'; a commander begins the game in the command zone (CR 903.6), and the command zone is not the hand. The claim that this cheats The Ur-Dragon into play is refuted — from there the rules offer one route, casting it for nine plus tax (CR 903.8). Everything below the command zone is affirmed: Drakuseth enters for {R}, its ability triggers because it attacks and not because it was cast (CR 508.3a), and damage already dealt is a one-shot effect the mandatory sacrifice cannot undo (CR 610.1). Hellkite Courser is the card in this deck whose text names the command zone.
combo_lines.006: The point of law is a window most players never name: CR 118.2 gives you a chance to activate mana abilities while paying a cost, and a Treasure's sacrifice is a mana ability that never uses the stack (CR 605.1a, 605.3b). Five Treasures therefore pay {3}{R}{R} in the middle of the activation, lands untouched. Seven in per connection, five out per activation — the ledger runs +2 a cycle. The holding: this loop is bounded by the game rather than the mana, since winning ends it mid-trigger (CR 104.2a).

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: Your discount engine, and it works from the command zone — every other Dragon spell costs {1} less whether or not he ever lands. Cast him when nine mana is genuinely spare; the attack trigger that draws a card per Dragon and drops a free permanent is the bonus, not the plan.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: One connection rolls a d20 and hands you that many flying bodies, which is the deck's biggest single-swing burst with Dragon Tempest out (stack 001). Send it at the emptiest board, not the scariest.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two-mana any-colour fixing in a five-colour deck. It belongs on turn two ahead of almost anything else you could do.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Costs {1} less per creature on the board, so it is usually a one-mana reset when the table has grown past you. With Wrathful Red Dragon out it stops being a reset and becomes an execution (stack 004).
card_roles.Boros Charm: Four to the face, indestructible for everything you own, or double strike on a Dragon — pick the mode that ends the turn. The indestructible mode is your cheapest way through a sweeper.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: Digs to the first nonland card and casts it free at mana value 8 or less, which describes most of your top end. Fire it when you need a body now, not when you want value.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: Costs {X} less for the artifacts opponents control, so it lands early against Treasure and equipment decks and mints Treasures back on every hit. Its pairing with Aggravated Assault still needs a stack scenario — take the body, not the promise.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: Your only clean answer to a resolved artifact or enchantment you otherwise cannot touch, and it hits anything at all. Aim it at the permanent that stops your combats.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: Turns every land you control into an any-colour source, which is worth far more than the mana it makes itself. Play it before the turn you need a double-pip spell, not on it.
card_roles.Counterspell: Two mana to say no. Hold it for someone's win attempt, not for the first scary creature you see.
card_roles.Crux of Fate: Choose destroy all non-Dragon creatures and it is a one-sided sweeper that leaves your board standing. Only take the other mode when someone else's Dragons have outgrown yours.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: Counters the noncreature spell and cannot be countered itself. Save it for the combo piece or the sweeper — the two things that actually beat you.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Every Dragon spell you cast is free while this is out. Land it and empty your hand the same turn, because the table will not let you keep it.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: Two mana, and every Dragon entering afterwards throws damage equal to your Dragon count. Get it down before the Dragons — it pays nothing for what already landed.
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour fixing that grows a gold counter per Dragon entering, and each counter cashes for a card. Play it early enough that the counters have time to stack.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: Three damage clears a small board on arrival, then every land drop becomes a 4/4 flier. It is your best single answer to a token pod.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Cannot be countered and shuts off opposing spells on your turn — this is the body you cast into open blue mana. It also makes your alpha strike safe from instant-speed tricks.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: Haste for the whole team, which turns every fresh Dragon into damage the turn it lands. Treat the 10-life punisher clause as a bonus, never a plan.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: {2} off every Dragon spell for three mana — the best turn-three play in the deck. Keep opening hands that contain it.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every time it attacks, before blockers ever matter. Cheat it in with Sneak Attack on the turn you need that damage immediately (stack 005).
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blinks your team out of a sweeper and returns them at end of turn, re-firing every enters trigger on the way back. Hold it as protection first and value second.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics on arrival, and it bounces itself when a Dragon enters, so it is ramp you replay. Cast it on four when nothing better exists.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana finds Aggravated Assault, Panharmonicon or the protection artifact you are missing. Cast it a turn before you need the card, never on the turn you do.
card_roles.Farseek: Fetches any nonbasic with a basic land type, which includes the shocks and the Triomes in this list. It fixes and ramps in the same two mana.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free while you control a commander, and your whole team becomes indestructible. Never let it rot in hand while you decline to commit the board.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for the team and a card every time a 4-power creature lands, which is nearly every creature you play. This is the draw engine your role budget is short on.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroys any permanent for three mana and hands back a 3/3. Spend it on the thing that beats you, not on the biggest body at the table.
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: A hasty 5-power flier that mints a Treasure whenever it attacks or gets targeted, and its Treasures make two mana each. That is unrestricted mana, so it can pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: This is the card that genuinely cheats The Ur-Dragon out of the command zone — hasty, for one attack, with the eminence draw trigger live and no tax (stack 005). Attack with everything the turn it enters.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: {1} off every Dragon plus a free look at the top of your library each upkeep. Name Dragon and never think about it again.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana buys hexproof and indestructible for everything you own. Hold it for the turn you commit the wave.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attacking adds mana equal to your attackers' total power, which is enormous and strictly for casting spells. Spend it on a second Dragon postcombat; it can never pay an activated ability.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Every nontoken Dragon after her drags a 5/5 along, and her pump ability converts a stalled board into lethal. Under Miirym and Panharmonicon one cast is 64 damage (stack 002).
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: Copies every nontoken Dragon you land after her, behind ward {2}. Sequence her ahead of the top end and expect the table to answer her first.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Free any-colour mana the moment you control a Dragon. Keep a Dragon on the battlefield and this is a land you never had to draw.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: Two mana for any Forest card, untapped — your Forest-typed duals included. It fixes and ramps without the tapped-land tax.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Every point of combat damage your team deals comes back as Treasure, and Treasure is the one mana here that can pay Aggravated Assault. With Assault out, a single unblocked connection ends the whole table (stack 006).
card_roles.Panharmonicon: Doubles every trigger caused by a creature entering — Miirym, Lathliss, Terror, Tempest, all of it (stack 002). Play it before the wave, never after.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: Name Dragon and everything you have lost comes back at once, including whatever a sweeper just ate. Save it for after the wrath, not before.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour mana, and it taps your legendary Dragons for more of it. In a list this legendary-dense that is a Signet that grows.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw cards equal to your biggest non-Human's power — often five or seven — or pump the team for the kill. It is an instant, so cast it after blockers are declared.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: A giant refill off your largest body plus a free spell at mana value 5 or less. Cast it with Terror of the Peaks or Scourge of Valkas still in hand.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two mana in any colours toward Dragon creature spells, and one Dragon recast from your graveyard each turn. That mana is spells-only — it will never pay Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Two mana to draw two and discard one, and it returns to your hand whenever a Dragon enters. Replay it every turn you have spare mana lying around.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Instant-speed tutor for any Dragon in the deck, engine piece or answer body. Cast it at the end of the turn before your big one.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Attacking adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} that survives the phase change, which is a whole extra Dragon in your postcombat main. With Aggravated Assault it pays for its own extra combat and leaves {R} behind (stack 003).
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Damage equal to your Dragon count every time a Dragon enters, itself included. It is Dragon Tempest on a body, so land it before the flood rather than during it.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Attack the player at the highest life and you untap your attackers for a free extra combat, once each turn. Point the first attack at the table leader deliberately.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forest cards onto the battlefield untapped on turn four, and your Forest-typed duals qualify. It fixes while it ramps.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colourless on turn one or two. Always keep it, always resolve it first.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana answers the sweeper, the ritual or the enchantment; they get a 2/2 flier and you keep your board. That trade is almost always yours.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: One mana exiles anything, which is the cleanest answer in the 99. Spend it on the creature that beats you, not on the first one you meet.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: Your board phases out and your life cannot change until your next turn. Hold it for the sweeper or the lethal swing — it is the best card you can have in hand on your big turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for everything and a card whenever a 4-power creature enters. Every Dragon you cast attacks the same turn it lands.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: Every creature entering afterwards throws its power at any target, and opponents pay three life just to target it. Land it first, then flood the board.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Attacking doubles the power of every Dragon you control, which is the fastest route from a fair board to a lethal one. Count damage before you declare attackers; it usually kills somebody.
card_roles.Tiamat: Casting it fetches five differently named Dragons straight to hand — take the engine pieces, not the biggest bodies. Eminence and the reducers make the seven-drop honest.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: {2} off every Dragon creature spell for three mana. Alongside Dragonspeaker Shaman it turns your top end into midrange.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: Every attacking Dragon brings a 6/6 flier with it, so one combat under this ends most boards. Keep it alive through a turn cycle and the long game is yours.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana at instant speed for any creature in the deck. Fetch the piece the turn before you need it, not the turn you are already dead.
card_roles.Aggravated Assault: The win condition and the loudest tell in one card: {3}{R}{R} untaps your team and buys another combat, and every infinite in the 99 runs through it. Hold it for the turn it kills someone, and remember your Dragon-restricted mana cannot pay the activation.
card_roles.Korlessa, Scale Singer: Two mana lets you cast Dragons straight off the top of your library, with the top card always visible. Every discount you control stacks onto those casts.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free while you control a commander, and it re-aims any spell or ability — the removal pointed at Aggravated Assault, or a tutor's target. Keep a red source up on the turns that matter.
card_roles.Wrathful Red Dragon: Damage dealt to your Dragons gets thrown back at any non-Dragon target, so a sweeper becomes an execution: three Dragons dealt 13 is 39 at one opponent (stack 004). Let them cast the wrath.
card_roles.Sneak Attack: One red mana puts any Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, and every attack and enters trigger fires before the end-step sacrifice (stack 005). It reaches your hand only, so never plan on it for the commander.
card_roles.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: A four-mana flier that pays when it dies — two cards to play, or three Treasures that pay for anything. Block with it happily.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Pay the 2 life and take it untapped; black is your scarcest colour on curve and the tempo beats the life every time.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Your untapped green-blue source for Korlessa or Miirym on curve. The 2 life is cheap on the turns those matter.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Green and white, untapped once two basics are down. Lead with basics early and this stops costing you a turn.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Red and green untapped once you control two basics — the two colours this deck leans on hardest.
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour, untapped, for one damage a tap. In a five-colour deck that is the cheapest fixing you will ever buy.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Red and white untapped as long as a Mountain or Plains is already down. Sequence your basics so it is.
card_roles.Command Tower: Any of your five colours, untapped, no cost at all. Play it the moment you draw it.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Reads your opponents' lands, so it is a second Command Tower at a multicolour table and much less at a mono-colour one. Check the board before you build a turn on it.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetches a basic and untaps it once four lands are down. Use it to grab the colour you are actually missing, not the one you have.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour untapped, and each tap hands an opponent a 1/1. Tap it when the mana matters more than the chump blocker you are giving away.
card_roles.Forest: Green for Nature's Lore, Farseek and the green half of Savage Ventmaw. Green is your most reliable colour precisely because of these.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: White and blue untapped if a Plains or Island is already down — your two thinnest colours, so play it on a turn you can afford tapped.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or any colour that may only cast a Dragon creature spell, plus a late buy-back for a dead Dragon. Never count its coloured mana toward an activated ability.
card_roles.Island: Your only blue basic — the Counterspell and Korlessa source. Fetch it with Fabled Passage when you are holding either.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: Three colours on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when you are flooded. Play it on a turn you were not going to spend everything anyway.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Colourless, or Dragon-spell-only colour, and it can sacrifice itself later to find a Dragon. Like Haven, its coloured mana casts and never activates.
card_roles.Mountain: Your most-demanded colour on a land that always comes in untapped. Fetch these first when a triple-red spell is in hand.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Black and green untapped for 2 life. Black sources are scarce enough here that you almost always pay.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Enters tapped, but every creature it casts that shares a type with your commander scries — which is nearly every spell you cast. Drop it on a turn you were not spending all your mana.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Copies whatever your other lands can make, so it is excellent late and nearly blank on turn one. Hold it behind a real dual when you can.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Red and green untapped once a Mountain or Forest is down. Sequence basics first and it never costs you tempo.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Three colours, always tapped. Play it on a turn where the tapped land costs you nothing.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Blue and red for 2 life. Take it untapped whenever you want Counterspell live this turn cycle.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Red and green for 2 life — the two colours your curve leans on hardest, so pay it more often than not.
card_roles.Sulfur Falls: Blue and red untapped once an Island or Mountain is down. It is your smoothest way to hold up a counter and cast a Dragon.
card_roles.Swamp: Your single black basic, and the fetch target that turns on Patriarch's Bidding or Crux of Fate. Go get it when either is in hand.
card_roles.The World Tree: Green while it is alone, and all-colour fixing for every land you control once six are down. Its ten-mana ability puts Tiamat onto the battlefield — the only God in the 99.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Name Dragon and it makes any colour for your creature spells. That mana casts; it never activates.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: Black, red and green on a tapped land, or a {3} cycle when your lands are already plentiful. Take the fixing early and the cycle late.

mulligan:
You have seen the shape now: 34 lands, a hump at three and a shelf of fives through sevens. Keeping seven means two to four lands and one piece of acceleration. Not two lands and a seven-drop.

The acceleration that decides games is a cost reducer. Ramp or fixing arrives by turn six in 71.6% of games; a reducer in only 33.2% — so when Dragonspeaker Shaman, Urza's Incubator or Herald's Horn is already in your opener, stop reading and keep. Reducer plus ramp together, the hand that casts a turn-five Ur-Dragon, shows up by turn six 23.1% of the time. Do not ship one of those hunting for prettier Dragons.

The second thing to want is a payoff before your first Dragon. Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising, Roiling Dragonstorm, Korlessa. A payoff is drawn by turn six in 62.2% of games; having one on turn two is how you beat that average instead of matching it.

Never mulligan for the commander. Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that can eventually cast him is worth nothing over a hand that cannot.

Ship two shapes. Hands that are lands plus top end with no bridge at three — land drops decay to 49.7% by turn six, so the bridge is not coming. And hands whose colours cannot cast their own spells: black fails you most often, at 11 land sources and 26.1% on curve, and Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw and Klauth only ever pay for spells.

Aggravated Assault in the opener is a hold, not a keep-reason; it needs a board and funding, and it does nothing on turn three but announce you. Protection is a real keep-bonus — Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver — because holding one is what lets you commit the wave later, and one is in hand by turn six in 66.0% of games.

Trust your sevens. The simulator keeps 75.1% of them and averages 0.313 mulligans, which means the hand in front of you is usually the hand. Mulligan for function, never for glamour.
upgrades:
Three contained two-card infinites; one enchantment carries all of them. That single figure ranks everything below it — a lone Naturalize is worth three kill lines here — so seven of the ten scouts are a second card name for the architecture stacks 003 and 006 already proved, not a new idea bolted on.

The cheapest of them costs three mana. The Reaver Cleaver puts 'create that many Treasures' onto an equipment instead of one specific seven-drop, and its pairing with the Assault already sleeved is the most popular line any candidate opens: 34,407 decks. Hellkite Charger runs the other direction — an extra combat printed on a Dragon body, so the eminence discount and every Dragon-restricted source reach the cast, even though its {5}{R}{R} activation still lands outside what that mana can pay.

Two more numbers worth sitting with. Three Visits traces to Skyshroud Claim at 0.9983 similarity for half the mana value, which is the same fetch two turns earlier in a deck whose ramp already shows up by turn six 71.6% of the time. And the deepest hole in the role budget is draw at minus six — that is the whole reason an eight-mana Dragon that draws a d20 of cards makes a ten-name list.

One caveat, sized honestly. Every combo line on the list reads 'needs a stack scenario', and no pick moves the computed floor off 4 — the bracket is already paid for, so nothing here is a power purchase. Popularity counts how many people believe a line; the verified stamps sit only on the engines already in the 99, and one of those numbers is evidence.
mana_base:
Thirty-four lands, sixteen of them entering tapped. That is 47% against a one-in-three budget, and the audit flags it — the toll for five colours standing behind a nine-mana commander. The goldfish shows where the bill lands: 3.042 mana on turn three, 4.937 on turn six, 6.539 on turn ten. This deck rarely misses a colour. It misses turns.

Pip share and source share disagree most on red. Red is 46.5% of the pip load carried by 28.6% of the sources — 47 red pips across 32 cards, as many as three at once. Green is nearly square, 21.8% of pips on 25.7% of sources, and it is the colour whose lands keep up: 84.9% on curve from lands alone against red's 58.0%, because green asks one pip at a time where red's effective ask is two.

Black is the genuine hole, and it is a small one by weight: 7.9% of the pips, 11 land sources, 26.1% on curve. Blue and white sit at 67.0% and 63.3% off 11 and 10 land sources, which is the quiet luxury of colours that only ever ask for one pip.

Six rocks and three dorks are what close those gaps, and they close them unevenly — black to 44.6%, red to 76.4%, white to 78.7%, blue to 81.0%, green to 92.7%. Five of the nine make any colour at all: Arcane Signet, Chromatic Lantern, Dragon's Hoard, Mox Jasper, Relic of Legends. In a base this stretched, the fixing package is doing the colour work and the land count is doing the mana.

Then the yardstick, which is worth reading correctly. A 90% on-curve rate would want 36 black and 36 red sources inside a 34-land deck — a measuring stick, not a possibility, and it reads that way in any five-colour list. Two things the audit refuses to count: five sources make spells-only mana, which is real for casting and worth nothing to an activated ability, and Treasures out of Old Gnawbone, Goldspan Dragon, Atsushi and Cavern-Hoard Dragon are unrestricted income no opponent can forecast from your board.
